newsitem.title: USA: Discovery crew to give Hubble telescope a tune-up.
newsitem.headline: Discovery crew to give Hubble telescope a tune-up.

text.p: Shuttle Discovery and its crew prepared to blast off on Tuesday to tune up the $1.6 billion Hubble Space Telescope by swapping out ageing scientific instruments and installing advanced devices that will let astronomers peer farther into the universe.

Weather forecasters kept a close eye on clouds that drifted across Florida's central coast and threatened to delay the launch scheduled for 3:55 a.m. EST (8:55 GMT). The shuttle has a 65-minute window for launch on Tuesday.

"The concern might be for some clouds in the Kennedy Space Centre area," said Lisa Malone, a spokeswoman for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. "The final inspection team is continuing to make its assessment out at the launch pad."

Commander Ken Bowersox and six other astronauts will spend 10 days in space to service and upgrade the Hubble telescope that was released into orbit in 1990. Four spacewalks are scheduled to install new scientific instruments and swap out some of the telescope's outdated parts such as a reel-to-reel tape recorder.
The crew was scheduled to begin boarding the shuttle shortly after 1 a.m. EST (0600 GMT).
The most important tasks of the high-tech service call will be to install two new scientific instruments, both about the size of a telephone booth.
The first instrument, its detectors chilled to minus 355 degrees Fahrenheit (-215C), will give astronomers a chance to see farther into the universe than ever before using infrared light.

The second device, a spectrograph, will allow the Hubble telescope to gather data about the composition, motion and velocity of distant objects in unprecedented detail. It will be particularly useful for the detection of black holes.

Discovery's crew spent the past two years practicing the delicate repair and servicing work needed on the mission. One of the most difficult tasks will be to work around the telescope's delicate wing-like solar panels called arrays, which have become fragile and twisted in the harsh environment of space. Without electrical power the telescope would be rendered useless.
During some tasks, the shuttle's robot arm will come as close as eight inches (20 cm) to the arrays as it moves astronauts to their work sites on the telescope.
The Hubble telescope was designed to operate in space for 15 years, with a total of four servicing missions by shuttle crews to keep the observatory functioning smoothly.

In 1993, NASA astronauts were dispatched to the telescope to successfully repair its blurred vision and help restore the space agency's tarnished reputation. The telescope has worked well since that visit, and has revolutionised astronomers' vision of the galaxy and provided more clues to the age and size of the universe.

NASA cleared the shuttle for launch after determining that mysterious oxygen readings in Discovery's fuselage did not indicate a tiny leak. Technicians delayed filling the orbiter's giant fuel tank to finish troubleshooting the fuel cell system, which combines supercold liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen to generate electrical power.

"It's puzzling, but they do not think it's bad enough to keep us on the ground," said Bruce Buckingham, a spokesman for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. "We'll monitor it throughout the night."
Engineers suspected the high oxygen could be due to false readings from the shuttle's gas detectors or that nitrogen gas used to ventilate the fuselage contained some air.
